title: From Bacterial Memory to Gene Editing
topic: bacterial adaptive immunity and gene editing
paragraphs: In the late 1980s a team sequencing a bacterial gene ran past its end and found something nobody could explain.
Downstream of the gene sat a short sequence, roughly thirty base pairs long, repeated again and again.
Between one copy of the repeat and the next lay a stretch of similar length that was not repeated at all, and every one of those intervening stretches was different.
The arrangement was far too regular to be an accident.
The finding was published, noticed by a few specialists, and then left alone for fifteen years.
As sequencing grew cheap the same pattern surfaced everywhere.
Something like four in ten sequenced bacteria carried such an array, and the large majority of archaea did too.
By 2002 the arrangement had a formal name, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats, and an acronym that has since escaped the laboratory.
Two details hinted that the arrays were doing work.
They sat beside a tight cluster of genes encoding proteins that looked like nucleases and helicases, the enzymes that cut and unwind nucleic acids.
And the nonrepeating stretches between the repeats, called spacers, differed from strain to strain within one species.
The answer arrived around 2005, when several groups stopped comparing spacers with the host genome and began comparing them with everything else in the sequence databases.
The matches were not bacterial.
They came from bacteriophages, the viruses that prey on bacteria, and from plasmids, the small mobile circles of DNA that pass between cells.
A spacer was a fragment of something that had once tried to get in.
An array was a ledger of past intrusions, kept in the order they happened.
A ledger implies a use, and within two years the use was demonstrated.
In a dairy bacterium used to ferment yogurt and cheese, cultures were challenged with a phage and the survivors sequenced.
The survivors had added new spacers, and those spacers matched the attacking phage.
Deleting a single spacer from a resistant strain cost it protection against precisely the phage that spacer matched, and nothing else.
Adding a spacer to a strain that had never met the phage handed it protection it had not earned.
The defense was sequence specific, heritable, and acquired during an encounter rather than carried from birth.
That last property is what made the result startling.

Bacteria were already known to defend themselves, mainly with restriction enzymes, which cleave any DNA carrying a particular short sequence unless the cell has chemically marked its own copies as friendly.
That defense is blunt and fixed: the same weapon, aimed the same way, in every generation.
The arrays described something else.
A cell met a specific virus, kept a souvenir of it, and passed that souvenir to descendants who would know the virus on sight without ever having met it.
The cycle has three stages, and keeping them separate prevents most of the confusion around the subject.
In adaptation, the cell samples an invader and files a new spacer.
In expression, the array is transcribed and cut into small guide RNAs.
In interference, a guide loaded into a protein finds the matching sequence in an invading genome and cuts it.
Only the third stage resembles editing, and only the first two explain how the system knows what to aim at.
Adaptation is the rarest of the three and the least understood.
A pair of conserved proteins, Cas1 and Cas2, form a complex that captures a short piece of foreign DNA, called a protospacer, and installs it in the array.
The insertion is not random.
New spacers go in at one particular end, beside a stretch called the leader, so the array accumulates chronologically with the most recent threat at the front.
Each insertion also duplicates one copy of the repeat, which is why the alternating pattern survives every time the record grows.
Expression begins with a single long transcript.
The cell reads the whole array, repeats and spacers together, into one RNA molecule and then chops it into units.
Each mature guide carries about twenty nucleotides of spacer derived sequence, the part that will pair with a target, attached to a piece of repeat derived sequence that the protein grips.
In the best studied version a second small RNA, made elsewhere in the same locus, pairs with the repeat portion and is required both for chopping the long transcript and for the guide to function.
Interference is where the numbers get specific.
The loaded protein does not read the genome from one end to the other.
It collides with DNA at random, and at each collision it checks for a motif just two or three bases long.
Only when it finds one does it pry the double helix open and offer its guide to the exposed strand.
Pairing begins at the ten or twelve bases nearest the motif, a stretch called the seed, and if those fail to match the protein lets go within milliseconds.
If they match, pairing runs the length of the guide, the displaced strand loops out, and two nuclease domains inside the protein cut one strand each.
The product is a clean break across both strands, three base pairs from the motif.
That short motif is the hinge of the whole system.
It is called the protospacer adjacent motif.
In the most widely used version it is any base followed by two guanines, sitting immediately beside the target on the strand the guide does not pair with.
The motif is no part of the guide, and the requirement looks at first like a design flaw, since only sequences sitting next to the right two letters can be attacked.
It is not a flaw.
The spacer stored in the array is flanked by repeat sequence rather than by the motif, so a guide never finds the motif beside the cell's own copy of the record.
The motif licenses the cut, and by licensing it only outside the array it keeps the cell from shredding its own memory.
The same rule guides adaptation, where the capture complex prefers fragments carrying the motif.
Popular accounts reach immediately for scissors, and the metaphor does more harm than good.
In a bacterium the cut really is the end of the story: the invading genome has no future, the break destroys it, and most bacteria carry no pathway for stitching such a break back together.
In a nucleated cell the break is the beginning.
The cell notices the damage and repairs it, and what the experimenter gets is not the cut but whatever the repair machinery decides to do with it.
The scissors image describes the easy half of the job and skips the half that settles the outcome.
The step that turned a defense system into an instrument was smaller than the publicity suggests.
By 2012 it was clear that the two RNAs could be fused into one synthetic molecule, a single guide, and that the protein would work perfectly well with the fusion.
That left an enzyme whose specificity lived entirely in twenty nucleotides of RNA.
Earlier targeting tools had the same ambition but read DNA with protein, which meant building a new protein for every new site.
Retargeting the newer system means ordering a different short strand of RNA.
What happens after the break depends on which repair pathway arrives first.
The fast route rejoins the ends directly and often loses or gains a base or two along the way, which shifts the reading frame and silences the gene.
That is why gene knockouts are now routine.
The accurate route copies from a template, so a supplied donor sequence can install a chosen change, but it works mainly in dividing cells and is far less efficient.

One response has been to avoid double strand breaks entirely: editors that nick one strand and chemically convert a single base, and editors that nick one strand and write a short new sequence from an RNA template carried by the guide.
Specificity is the other honest worry.

Twenty bases is long enough to be unique in a mammalian genome in principle, but pairing tolerates mismatches, particularly at the end farthest from the motif, where one or two mismatched bases may not be enough to make the protein release.
A guide that behaves this way is promiscuous: it pairs where it was not sent and cuts sites that resemble its target without matching it.
The countermeasures are real and partial.

Engineered variants hold DNA less tightly and so demand a better match, shortened guides are less forgiving of mismatches, and a pair of nicking enzymes aimed at opposite strands severs the helix only where both bind.
Finding rare off target events among billions of cells remains a measurement problem of its own.
Delivery is the harder problem and the less glamorous one.
Taking cells out of a patient, editing them in a dish and returning them works, and it is where the first approved uses have landed, because the cells can be inspected before they go back.
Editing a tissue inside the body is another matter.

The most common viral vector carries roughly four and a half kilobases, and the gene for the standard enzyme alone runs about four, leaving no room for the promoter and guide it needs, which has pushed the field toward smaller enzymes borrowed from other bacteria.
Lipid particles sidestep the size limit but drain overwhelmingly to the liver.
And because these enzymes come from bacteria most people have already met, many patients carry antibodies and T cells primed against them.
The arc is worth holding in view.
A pattern that looked like sequencing noise turned out to be a filing system, the filing system a memory, and the memory a program that anyone can retype in twenty letters.
None of it was designed for human purposes, which is exactly why it works so well and exactly why it resists domestication.
Phages already carry proteins that shut the system down, a reminder that it has been under test far longer than it has been in use.
The instrument on the bench is a borrowed one, still carrying the constraints of the cell it came from.

questions.stem: According to the passage, where does a newly captured spacer end up in the array?
choices: Distributed at random among the spacers already stored there
At one end of the array, beside the leader sequence
At the end of the array farthest from the leader sequence
Inside the repeat that sits closest to the neighboring genes
In a second array kept separate from the original one

proof.quote: New spacers go in at one particular end, beside a stretch called the leader

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says outright that new spacers go in at one particular end, beside a stretch called the leader, which is what makes the array chronological.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 7 states directly that the insertion is not random, and then names the position.
Half right: it is one particular end, but paragraph 7 places it beside the leader rather than away from it.
Spacers sit between repeats, and paragraph 7 has each insertion duplicate a repeat rather than break into one.
No second array appears anywhere in the passage; the record grows inside the one array.

questions.stem: The passage states that when the bases nearest the motif fail to pair with the guide, the protein
choices: cuts one strand of the helix and leaves the other intact
opens a longer stretch of the helix and tries the match again
calls in a second protein to finish the search for a target
lets go of the DNA within milliseconds
files the mismatched sequence away as a new spacer

proof.quote: the protein lets go within milliseconds

questions.why: Paragraph 9 describes the seed, the ten or twelve bases nearest the motif, and says that if those fail to match the protein lets go within milliseconds.
distractorNotes: Single strand nicking shows up in paragraph 13 as a deliberate laboratory design, not as the response to a failed seed match.
Paragraph 9 runs the other way: the helix is opened first, and a failed seed ends the attempt.
No second protein is described at this step, and the two nuclease domains named in paragraph 9 are inside the same protein.
Filing a spacer belongs to adaptation in paragraph 7 and is carried out by a different pair of proteins.

questions.stem: In the phage experiment described, removing a single spacer from a resistant strain caused that strain to
choices: lose protection only against the phage that spacer matched
lose protection against every phage it had previously resisted
take up a replacement spacer from the surrounding medium
stop adding any new spacers to its array from then on
resist a wider range of phages than it had resisted before

proof.quote: cost it protection against precisely the phage that spacer matched, and nothing else

questions.why: Paragraph 4 reports that deleting one spacer cost the strain protection against precisely the phage that spacer matched, and nothing else.
distractorNotes: Too sweeping: paragraph 4 stresses that the loss was confined to the matching phage.
Paragraph 4 has spacers added during infection or by the experimenters, never picked up to fill a deletion.
The experiment measured protection, and the passage never claims that deletion shuts adaptation down.
This reverses the finding: the deletion cost protection instead of broadening it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the trouble with the most common viral vector is that
choices: patients have usually been exposed already to the bacteria it comes from
it delivers almost all of its cargo to the liver
it has to be given over and over again before a useful number of cells are edited
it works only in cells that are actively dividing
its capacity leaves no room for the promoter and guide beside the enzyme gene

proof.quote: leaving no room for the promoter and guide it needs

questions.why: Paragraph 15 gives the numbers: the vector carries roughly four and a half kilobases and the enzyme gene alone runs about four, so the promoter and guide do not fit.
distractorNotes: Prior exposure in paragraph 15 is to the bacteria the enzymes come from, not to the vector.
Draining to the liver is the drawback of lipid particles in that same paragraph, offered as the alternative.
Repeat dosing is never mentioned; the stated obstacle is size.
Dependence on dividing cells belongs to the template copying repair route in paragraph 13.

questions.stem: The passage reports that the repeat arrays sit next to
choices: the genes a cell uses to mark its own DNA as friendly rather than foreign
a long stretch of DNA that encodes no protein at all
a cluster of genes for proteins resembling nucleases and helicases
the plasmids that carry DNA between bacterial cells
a duplicated copy of the whole bacterial chromosome

proof.quote: a tight cluster of genes encoding proteins that looked like nucleases and helicases

questions.why: Paragraph 2 names this as one of the two details that hinted the arrays were doing work: they sat beside a tight cluster of genes for proteins that looked like nucleases and helicases.
distractorNotes: Marking one's own DNA as friendly belongs to the restriction enzyme system in paragraph 5, used there as a contrast.
Paragraph 2 says those neighboring genes encode proteins, which is exactly why they were suggestive.
Plasmids appear in paragraph 3 as a source of spacer sequence, not as a neighbor of the array.
No duplicated chromosome appears in the passage; paragraph 7 duplicates a single repeat.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 10, "licenses" most nearly means
choices: explains
permits
measures
conceals
postpones

proof.quote: The motif licenses the cut, and by licensing it only outside the array

questions.why: In paragraph 10 the motif licenses the cut, meaning it gives the cut permission to proceed, and withholding that permission inside the array is what protects the cell's own record.
distractorNotes: The motif does not account for the cut, it allows it; the sentence is about permission rather than explanation.
Nothing is being quantified in that sentence, which is about whether cutting may go ahead.
The motif sits in plain view beside the target, and hiding it would defeat the checkpoint entirely.
The motif does not delay the cut, it is the condition that lets the cut happen at all.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 14, "promiscuous" most nearly means
choices: unusually quick to act
easily broken down
shortened at one end
not selective enough
present in many copies

proof.quote: it pairs where it was not sent and cuts sites that resemble its target without matching it

questions.why: Paragraph 14 defines the word in the same sentence: a promiscuous guide pairs where it was not sent and cuts sites that merely resemble its target.
distractorNotes: Speed is not at issue there; the sentence is about where a guide binds, not how fast.
Nothing about the guide breaking down appears in that paragraph, which is describing binding behavior.
Shortened guides turn up in the same paragraph as one of the fixes, so this trades the problem for the remedy.
Copy number is never discussed; the sentence concerns a single guide pairing in the wrong place.

questions.stem: Paragraph 10 most strongly supports which conclusion about a bacterium whose stored spacer happened to sit beside the recognition motif?
choices: It could no longer transcribe its array into guide RNAs
It would stop capturing new spacers from invading DNA
It would risk having its own record cut by one of its own guides
It would lose the ability to recognize the matching phage
It would need a second copy of the motif on the opposite strand before cutting

proof.quote: a guide never finds the motif beside the cell's own copy of the record
it keeps the cell from shredding its own memory

questions.why: Paragraph 10 explains that the stored spacer is flanked by repeat sequence rather than by the motif, which is what keeps a guide from attacking the array. Put the motif there and that protection is gone.
distractorNotes: Transcription is described in paragraph 8 and does not depend on the motif in any way.
Capture is described as preferring fragments that carry the motif, and nothing ties it to what is already stored.
Recognition comes from the twenty nucleotide guide, which would be unchanged; what changes is whether the array can be attacked.
The passage describes one motif, on the strand the guide does not pair with, and never a second.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about the same enzyme acting in a bacterium and in a nucleated cell does the passage best support?
choices: An identical cut can lead to different outcomes depending on the cell that receives it
The enzyme cuts less accurately once it is working inside a nucleated cell
The enzyme would require a different recognition motif in order to work inside a nucleated cell
A nucleated cell destroys the enzyme before it can ever reach its target
A bacterium repairs a double strand break more precisely than a nucleated cell does

proof.quote: In a bacterium the cut really is the end of the story
In a nucleated cell the break is the beginning.
whatever the repair machinery decides to do with it

questions.why: Paragraph 11 says the cut ends the story in a bacterium but only begins it in a nucleated cell, where the repair machinery decides what the experimenter actually gets.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 11 is about what follows the cut, not about cutting accuracy, which is raised separately in paragraph 14.
The motif is a property of the enzyme and its guide, and the passage never makes it depend on the host cell.
The immune recognition in paragraph 15 concerns patients carrying antibodies, not a cell destroying the enzyme at the target.
Paragraph 11 says most bacteria have no pathway for rejoining such a break, so they do not repair it more precisely.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central point of the passage?
choices: Repeated sequences found in bacterial genomes had no known function for fifteen years after they were first reported
Gene editing will stay impractical until viral vectors can be engineered to carry a much larger cargo
Bacterial defenses turn out to be more sophisticated than the immune memory found in vertebrate animals
The recognition motif is the single feature that matters most in the whole system, in bacteria and in the laboratory alike
A bacterial record of past infection was decoded and then borrowed as a tool that still carries its original constraints

proof.quote: An array was a ledger of past intrusions
the memory a program that anyone can retype in twenty letters
The instrument on the bench is a borrowed one, still carrying the constraints of the cell it came from.

questions.why: The passage moves from an unexplained pattern to a memory system to a laboratory instrument, and closes in paragraph 16 by calling that instrument borrowed and still bound by the cell it came from.
distractorNotes: True, and drawn from paragraphs 1 and 2, but far too narrow to carry sixteen paragraphs.
Vector capacity is one obstacle named in paragraph 15, not the claim the passage is built to make.
The passage compares the two kinds of defense without ranking bacteria above animals.
Paragraph 10 does call the motif the hinge of the system, but one mechanism is not the point of the whole piece.

questions.stem: Paragraph 5 is included mainly in order to
choices: explain how restriction enzymes pick out the sequences they cut
argue that restriction enzymes protect a cell less effectively than arrays do
show what sets the array system apart from the defense bacteria were already known to have
introduce the three stages of the cycle that the paragraph immediately after it goes on to list
establish that bacteria are attacked by plasmids as well as by viruses

proof.quote: That last property is what made the result startling.
That defense is blunt and fixed
The arrays described something else.

questions.why: Paragraph 5 sets a blunt, fixed, inherited defense against a specific memory of a specific attacker, and that contrast is what makes the earlier result startling.
distractorNotes: Recognition gets one clause there, as setup for the contrast rather than as the point of the paragraph.
The paragraph draws a difference in kind, blunt and fixed against specific and remembered, and never ranks the two.
The three stages arrive in paragraph 6, and paragraph 5 does not preview them.
That the invaders include both phages and plasmids is already established back in paragraph 3.

questions.stem: Which best describes the way the passage is organized?
choices: A laboratory technique is described first, then traced back to the organism it came from, then set against the rival techniques it displaced
An unexplained observation is reported, its function is worked out, its mechanism is detailed, and its move into the laboratory is assessed
A controversy is introduced, the evidence on both sides is weighed, and one side is finally endorsed
A series of experiments is presented in the order performed, each one correcting an error made in the one before it
A general principle is stated at the outset and then illustrated with examples of steadily increasing difficulty

proof.quote: found something nobody could explain
A ledger implies a use, and within two years the use was demonstrated.
The cycle has three stages
The step that turned a defense system into an instrument

questions.why: The passage opens on a puzzle in paragraph 1, settles what the arrays are for by paragraph 4, spends paragraphs 6 through 10 on mechanism, and then weighs the laboratory version in paragraphs 11 through 16.
distractorNotes: The passage runs the other way, from the bacterial observation forward to the technique, and rival tools get a single sentence in paragraph 12.
The author does push back on a popular metaphor in paragraph 11, but no two sided controversy is set up and weighed.
Experiments appear early, and the later work builds on the earlier work rather than correcting it.
The opening offers a puzzle rather than a principle, and nothing is laid down as a rule to be illustrated.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the habit of comparing the protein to a pair of scissors is best described as
choices: amused by a figure of speech that no specialist takes seriously
neutral, on the grounds that the comparison is accurate as far as it goes
enthusiastic about a phrase that makes a hard idea accessible to readers
impatient with it, because it drops the part that settles the result
alarmed by it, as a claim that has pushed researchers into unsafe work

proof.quote: the metaphor does more harm than good
skips the half that settles the outcome

questions.why: Paragraph 11 says the metaphor does more harm than good and ends by charging it with describing the easy half of the job and skipping the half that settles the outcome.
distractorNotes: Nothing in paragraph 11 is playful, and the author treats the metaphor as a live problem.
Calling the image harmful is the opposite of neutral.
The author presents the phrase as a source of confusion, not as a helpful simplification.
Too strong: the complaint is that the image is incomplete, and no researcher is accused of unsafe work.

questions.stem: In describing the measures taken against cutting at unintended sites, the author is best described as
choices: candid, treating the measures as genuine and the problem as still open
dismissive, treating the measures as amounting to very little in practice
confident, treating the problem as one the measures have brought under control
puzzled, treating the measures as working for reasons nobody has established
resigned, treating further progress on the problem as unlikely

proof.quote: The countermeasures are real and partial.
remains a measurement problem of its own

questions.why: Paragraph 14 calls the countermeasures real and partial in the same breath, lists three of them, and then notes that finding rare off target events is still a measurement problem of its own.
distractorNotes: The author calls the countermeasures real and describes three of them without belittling any.
The word partial, and the unsolved detection problem at the end, rule out any sense of control.
Paragraph 14 explains exactly why each measure works, so nothing there is presented as mysterious.
The author leaves the problem open rather than predicting that it will not improve.

questions.stem: The passage supports each of the following statements EXCEPT:
choices: The order of the spacers in an array carries information about when each threat was met.
The same protein can be aimed at a new target without altering the protein itself.
Cutting both strands of the helix is not required in order to change a single base.
Some viruses that infect bacteria can shut the system down.
A guide that matches its target perfectly will cut that sequence wherever it occurs.

proof.quote: the array accumulates chronologically with the most recent threat at the front
Retargeting the newer system means ordering a different short strand of RNA.
editors that nick one strand and chemically convert a single base
Phages already carry proteins that shut the system down
only sequences sitting next to the right two letters can be attacked

questions.why: Paragraph 10 makes a perfect match insufficient on its own: only sequences sitting next to the motif can be attacked, so a flawless guide is stopped wherever the motif is missing.
distractorNotes: Supported, so not the exception: paragraph 7 has new spacers enter at the leader end, making the array chronological.
Supported, so not the exception: paragraph 12 says retargeting means ordering a different short strand of RNA.
Supported, so not the exception: paragraph 13 describes editors that nick one strand and convert a base.
Supported, so not the exception: paragraph 16 notes that phages carry proteins that shut the system down.

questions.stem: A reader looking for an explanation of why the repeats stay evenly spaced as the record grows should turn to
choices: paragraph 1
paragraph 2
paragraph 7
paragraph 9
paragraph 13

proof.quote: which is why the alternating pattern survives every time the record grows

questions.why: Paragraph 7 supplies the reason: each insertion also duplicates one copy of the repeat, so the alternating pattern survives every time a spacer is added.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 1 describes the alternating pattern as it was first seen, without saying what maintains it.
Paragraph 2 reports how widespread the arrays are and what sits beside them.
Paragraph 9 is about finding and cutting a target, not about the structure of the array.
Paragraph 13 concerns what a cell does after a break, a different subject altogether.
